x: Option B is incorrect: malachite is the basic carbonate Cu₂(CO₃)(OH)₂, while Cu₂S is chalcocite. The haematite, pyrolusite and chalcopyrite formulas are right.
t: Discriminate sulphide, oxide and carbonate ores of copper.

x: Both are true and R explains A: very reactive metals cannot be reduced by carbon, so they are won by electrolysing their molten salts, or alumina in molten cryolite.
t: Recall the extraction method for each part of the reactivity series.

x: Galena is the ore of lead, cinnabar of mercury, cassiterite of tin and argentite of silver, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the metal in each ore.

x: All four are correct: lithium is the lightest metal, osmium the densest, tungsten among the hardest, and mercury the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
t: Recall the record-holding metals.

x: Both are true: iron rusts only with both oxygen and moisture, and the rust, hydrated Fe₂O₃, weighs more than the iron because it adds oxygen and water.
t: Recall the conditions and product of rusting.

x: Three occur native: gold, silver and platinum, because they are unreactive. Aluminium is very reactive and is found combined, mainly as bauxite.
t: Recall that unreactive metals occur free.

x: Duralumin is aluminium with copper, magnesium and manganese, light and strong for aircraft. Brass and bronze are copper alloys and nichrome is Ni–Cr.
t: Recall the make-up and use of each alloy.

x: Both are true and R explains A: roasting heats sulphide ores in excess air to turn them into oxides, which is why it is used for sulphides.
t: Discriminate roasting (sulphides, air) from calcination (carbonates, limited air).

x: Smelting gives molten metal by high-temperature reduction, calcination heats carbonate ores in limited air, froth flotation concentrates sulphides, and carbon reduces less reactive metals, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall each metallurgical step.

x: All four are correct in the order K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au: copper is above mercury, so III is true too. The given key wrongly left out III.
t: Recall the reactivity series in order.

x: Both are true: ilmenite is found in beach sands from Kerala to Odisha, and Bailadila in Chhattisgarh is famous for high-grade haematite.
t: Recall where each Indian ore occurs.

x: Sodium vapour gives the yellow glow of street lights, and liquid sodium cools the Fast Breeder Test Reactor at Kalpakkam.
t: Recall the uses of sodium.

x: Bauxite, cryolite, corundum and diaspore are all aluminium minerals, so every item pairs with (i).
t: Recall the ores of aluminium.

x: Both are true: chalcopyrite, chalcocite, cuprite, malachite and azurite are all copper ores.
t: Recall the ores of copper.

x: All four are zinc ores: zinc blende, smithsonite, zincite and franklinite.
t: Recall the ores of zinc.

x: Both are true: cerargyrite (horn silver) and native silver give silver, while rock salt, trona and Chile saltpetre are sodium ores.
t: Recall the ores of silver and sodium.

x: I, II and III are correct: carnallite (KCl·MgCl₂·6H₂O) is an ore of both potassium and magnesium, and magnesite and dolomite are magnesium ores. IV is false because limestone is a calcium ore.
t: Recall carnallite as a double ore of K and Mg.

x: Three are manganese ores: pyrolusite, manganite and hausmannite. Ilmenite is a titanium ore.
t: Recall the ores of manganese.

x: All five are iron ores: haematite (most common), magnetite, limonite, siderite and iron pyrites.
t: Recall the ores of iron.

x: Both are true: chalcopyrite is also called copper pyrites, and chalcocite and cuprite are main copper ores.
t: Recall the ores of copper.

x: All eight are correct: malachite and azurite are copper ores, galena and cerussite lead ores, and zinc blende (black jack), smithsonite and zincite zinc ores.
t: Recall the ores of copper, lead and zinc.

x: Cinnabar is the mercury ore, cassiterite the tin ore, argentite is called silver glance and cerargyrite horn silver, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the ores and their other names.

x: All four are correct: rock salt is a sodium ore, sylvine and carnallite potassium ores, and magnesite and dolomite magnesium ores.
t: Recall the ores of alkali and alkaline earth metals.

x: Two are calcium ores: limestone and calcite. Cinnabar is mercury ore and cassiterite tin ore.
t: Recall the ores of calcium.

x: Both are true: bauxite is hydrated aluminium oxide, and haematite is an iron ore, Fe₂O₃.
t: Recall the composition of major ores.

x: All three are correct: magnetite, Fe₃O₄, is an iron ore and is naturally magnetic.
t: Recall the iron oxide ores.

x: Galena (PbS) is lead, cinnabar (HgS) mercury, chalcopyrite copper and zinc blende (ZnS) zinc, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the sulphide ores.

x: Cassiterite (SnO₂) is tin, argentite (Ag₂S) silver, rock salt (NaCl) sodium and carnallite contains potassium and magnesium, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the formula and metal of each ore.

x: Both are correct: gypsum is CaSO₄·2H₂O and fluorspar is CaF₂, and both are calcium minerals.
t: Recall the calcium minerals.

x: All four are correct: monazite is a thorium mineral in Indian beach sands, and ilmenite is a titanium mineral of coastal sands.
t: Recall India's beach-sand minerals.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: being a magnesium silicate does not by itself make talc soft; its weakly bonded layers do.
t: Check whether R is the cause or only the composition.

x: Magnetite is Fe₃O₄, limonite FeO(OH)·nH₂O, siderite FeCO₃ and iron pyrites FeS₂, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the formulas of iron ores.

x: Both are true: galena is PbS and cuprite is Cu₂O.
t: Recall the formulas of ores.

x: Zinc blende is ZnS, cinnabar HgS, cassiterite SnO₂ and argentite Ag₂S, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the formulas of ores.

x: Rock salt is NaCl, carnallite KCl·MgCl₂·6H₂O, magnesite MgCO₃ and dolomite CaMg(CO₃)₂, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall the formulas of ores.

x: All four are correct: limestone and calcite are both CaCO₃, gypsum is CaSO₄·2H₂O and fluorspar CaF₂.
t: Recall the calcium minerals.

x: Both are true and R explains A: iron and copper are got as molten metal by reducing their ores at high temperature, which is smelting.
t: Check whether R defines the process in A.

x: Both are listed as true: the Bayer process purifies bauxite into alumina, and the Hall-Héroult process electrolyses it to give aluminium.
t: Discriminate Bayer (refining) from Hall-Héroult (electrolysis).

x: All four are correct: iron, zinc, tin and lead sit in the middle of the series and are reduced from their oxides by carbon.
t: Recall which metals carbon can reduce.

x: All four are correct: sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife and are highly reactive alkali metals.
t: Recall the properties of alkali metals.

x: All five are correct: gold is the most malleable, ductile and least reactive metal, silver the best conductor, lead a poor heat conductor, aluminium the most abundant metal in the crust and diamond the hardest natural substance.
t: Recall the record properties of metals.

x: In the series Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe, sodium is above calcium, calcium above magnesium, magnesium above aluminium and zinc above iron, giving a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii.
t: Recall the reactivity series in order.

x: Both are true: in the order Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag, iron beats lead, lead beats hydrogen, hydrogen beats copper and mercury beats silver.
t: Recall the reactivity series in order.

x: All four are aluminium uses: aircraft, cookware, electrical cables and packaging foil.
t: Recall the uses of aluminium.

x: Iron and steel are used mainly in construction, tools and vehicles. "Only" makes options A and D wrong, and packaging uses aluminium.
t: Check each option for the word "only".

x: Iron and steel build vehicles, copper makes wiring, zinc galvanises iron and tin goes into solder, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall the use of each metal.

x: Both are true: iron and steel make tools and infrastructure, and copper makes utensils and alloys.
t: Recall the uses of common metals.

x: All three are correct: zinc is used in alloys such as brass, and tin plating coats food cans.
t: Recall the uses of zinc and tin.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: barometers are a separate use, while mercury suits thermometers because it expands evenly and stays liquid.
t: Check whether R is a cause or a parallel use.

x: All three are correct: gold, silver and platinum are used in coins, electronics and as catalysts.
t: Recall the uses of noble metals.

x: Brass is Cu + Zn, bronze Cu + Sn, stainless steel Fe + Cr + Ni and nichrome Ni + Cr, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the composition of each alloy.

x: Brass is used in utensils and decoration, bronze in coins and statues, stainless steel in utensils and surgical tools, and nichrome in heating elements, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the use of each alloy.

x: Tungsten is very hard with the highest melting point of any metal, so it is used in hard tools and bulb filaments. Nichrome is for heating elements.
t: Recall the uses of tungsten.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: joining metals is the use, while the tin–lead mix is chosen for its low melting point.
t: Check whether R explains the composition or only the use.

x: Both are true: K, Na, Ca, Mg and Al are too reactive to occur free, while Au, Ag, Pt and copper sit low in the series and can occur native.
t: Recall that reactivity decides whether a metal occurs free.

x: Both are true and R explains A: silver reacts with H₂S in the air to form black silver sulphide, Ag₂S, which is the tarnish.
t: Check whether R is the reaction behind A.

x: Galvanising coats iron with zinc, anodising grows an Al₂O₃ layer on aluminium, tin plating prevents corrosion and food cans are tin-plated, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the methods of preventing corrosion.

x: Ilmenite is FeTiO₃, corundum Al₂O₃, ruby is corundum coloured by chromium and cryolite is Na₃AlF₆, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the formulas of minerals.

x: Potassium is at the top of the series and reacts violently with cold water, giving KOH and hydrogen. Zinc, tin and copper do not react with cold water.
t: Recall the reactivity series.

x: Both are true: paint and oil form a barrier that keeps air and moisture away from iron.
t: Recall the barrier methods of preventing rust.

x: All four are correct: sodium and potassium are kept under kerosene so they cannot react with air and moisture.
t: Recall how reactive metals are stored.

x: Titanium occurs as ilmenite, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh have thorium-bearing sands and copper occurs as sulphides, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i, though option C also fits since List-II repeats.
t: Recall that the code pairs items in order when List-II repeats.

x: All three are correct: zinc is more reactive than tin, so food cans use tin, which will not react with acidic foods.
t: Recall why food cans are tin-plated.

x: Bauxite is hydrated alumina, Al₂O₃·xH₂O. Plain Al₂O₃ is corundum and Na₃AlF₆ is cryolite.
t: Discriminate bauxite from corundum and cryolite.

x: All three are correct: monazite sands occur in Kerala and Odisha, and Na, K, Ca and Mg occur only combined, as salts or carbonates.
t: Recall India's beach-sand minerals.
